title: Checking Whether SCOS is up to SPEC
short_title: Checking whether SCOS is up to SPEC (certification)
organisation: European Space Agency, Directorate of Technical and Operational Support (ESTEC and ESOC), with TÜV InterTraffic
status_notes: Published magazine article (esa bulletin 115, august 2003, printed pages 58-60); running head 'Certification of SCOS-2000'.
summary:
A three-page ESA Bulletin article (August 2003) by F. Aldea (ESTEC), M. Jones and E. Gomez (ESOC) and H. Schäbe (TÜV InterTraffic) on the independent evaluation and certification of SCOS-2000 with SPEC (Software Product Evaluation and Certification), a method developed under ESA contract and based on several international standards. SCOS-2000 was the largest product evaluated with SPEC to date.

It explains the SPEC quality model: goal properties (such as functionality) split into second-level properties (completeness, correctness, efficiency), each quantified by metrics measured with defined evaluation methods. The model covers product properties (functionality, reliability, maintainability, re-usability, operability, documentation quality) and process properties (suitability for safety, software development effectiveness, system engineering effectiveness), including space practices from ECSS-E-40 and ECSS-Q-80. A sidebar summarises SCOS-2000: a generic, distributed and scalable mission control system (down to a single-workstation 'SCOS-2000 in-a-box'), with telemetry processing, telecommanding, online database and archive, general services, the Operation Language, roles and privileges, events and actions and on-board software maintenance, configured per mission through its database and configuration files. More than 40 customer licences had been granted.

The Phase I baseline evaluation of version 2.1e found that, of 85 SPEC metrics, 10 were inapplicable, 3 were replaced and 5 of 72 missed their target, so improvement was needed before certification as Class-B (mission-critical) software. Recommendations covered documentation quality, traceability, architecture simplification and coding standards; a Phase II delta evaluation and certification were to follow, and SPEC was also being applied to RTEMS.

It is a short primary source on SCOS-2000's software quality status around 2003.

key_points.text: SCOS-2000, originally operational software for ESA missions, was being promoted as an ESA product and more than 40 customer licences had been granted.
Certification benchmarks the product against an agreed quality model, performed by an independent organisation (TÜV InterTraffic) using the SPEC method.
SPEC goal properties are split into properties quantified by metrics; efficiency, for example, is measured by timing margins, memory margins, throughput and resource utilisation.

SPEC product-related goal properties: functionality, reliability, maintainability, re-usability, operability, documentation quality; process-related: suitability for safety, software development effectiveness, system engineering effectiveness; it covers practices such as those of ECSS-E-40 and ECSS-Q-80.

SCOS-2000 functions listed: TM, TC, online database, online archive, general services and utilities, Operation Language (OL), roles and privileges (USER), events and actions (EVAC) and OBSM; the typical configuration is distributed but can be scaled down to 'SCOS-2000 in-a-box'.
Phase I evaluated baseline version 2.1e; Phase II is a delta evaluation and certification agreed between ESTEC, ESOC and TÜV.
Of the 85 metrics defined by SPEC, 10 were inapplicable, 3 were not measured and were replaced, and 5 out of 72 failed to reach the target value.
SCOS-2000 still needed improvement before it could be certified as Class-B (mission-critical) software.
Phase I was preceded by a Software Criticality Analysis based on a software FMECA, performed by Critical Software (Portugal).
New coding standards were to cover state-of-the-art methods such as Model Driven Architecture and the languages used to develop SCOS-2000, primarily C++ and Java.
